## The design

```systemverilog
logic [3:0] hist;      // the last four bits, oldest at the top
logic [2:0] fill;      // bits since reset, stopping at 4

wire [3:0] next_hist = {hist[2:0], din};

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (!rst_n) begin
        hist <= 4'b0; fill <= 3'd0; found <= 1'b0;
    end else begin
        hist  <= next_hist;
        if (fill != 3'd4) fill <= fill + 3'd1;
        found <= (fill >= 3'd3) && (next_hist == pattern);
    end
end
```

Three decisions in nine lines.

**The comparison is against `next_hist`.** `hist` is what the register
holds *now*, which is the four bits before this one. Comparing against
it would report a match one cycle after it happened. Naming the
post-edge value and comparing with that keeps `found` exactly one cycle
behind the last bit — which is what "registered" means and what the
testbench samples.

**`fill` is a saturating counter that only has to answer one question.**
Three bits is enough to hold 0 to 4, and once it reaches 4 it stays
there, so the comparison `fill >= 3` is true for ever afterwards. Note
that it still reads 3 at the edge that clocks in the fourth bit, because
a non-blocking assignment updates it at the end of the step.

**`found` is a register.** It is assigned inside the clocked block with
`<=`. The temptation is to write `assign found = (hist == pattern);`,
which is a cycle out *and* makes `found` combinational on `pattern`, so
changing the pattern mid-stream would retroactively produce a pulse.

## Why a shift register and not a state machine

The classic solution to "find a fixed pattern in a bit stream" is a
state machine whose state is *how much of the pattern has matched so
far* — the Knuth–Morris–Pratt construction. For `1011` it needs five
states and five flip-flops become three.

It cannot be used here, and the reason is the whole point of making
`pattern` an input. The state machine's next-state table is derived from
the pattern: from "matched `101`", a `0` goes to "matched `10`" because
`1010` ends in `10`. That derivation is done when the circuit is built.
With a runtime pattern there is nothing to derive it from, so the table
would itself have to be computed in hardware — which is far more logic
than the four flip-flops and the comparator this costs.

The trade is the usual one:

| | fixed pattern | runtime pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| state machine | $\lceil \log_2 (n{+}1)\rceil$ flip-flops | needs the table built in hardware |
| shift register | $n$ flip-flops and an $n$-bit comparator | the same, and the pattern is just a bus |

For four bits the shift register wins outright. For a 64-bit preamble
with a fixed value the state machine wins by a factor of ten, and real
receivers use one.

## The reset trap

`hist` comes out of reset holding `4'b0000`. If the pattern happens to
be `0000` — or if three zeros of reset plus one real bit happen to
complete it — a design without `fill` reports a match that never
occurred. The grading testbench sets `pattern = 0000`, resets, and
drives three zeros, which is the cheapest possible way to catch it.

It is a real bug class, not a puzzle. Any register whose reset value is
a legal data value needs something saying "this is not data yet", and
the something is almost always a counter or a valid bit.
